blocks.x: I'm going to play something. And they had some people from West Germany, and they recorded the one thing. And I was supposed to get one of the records and all that, and a little magazine from West Germany, which I never get from Joe, you know, from Joe Moran.

I may have that in a book, man. I may have your picture in a book, I might. From Germany. Was Pinky playing too much? Yeah. I think I have a picture of that. And you had a woman singing gospel songs? Right. Yeah. How is it, Betty? Is it a machine worker?
Yeah, I played, man.
Who's the loudest? Me and him? Speak again. Okay, say something, Sal. What's your name? Sal Guterres. He's got a little stronger than you are. That's good. What's your right name?

And in Salvador? Well, in Nashville, in Salvador. You got a middle name? Edward. Salvador Edward Gutierrez. Oh, what's today's date, by the way? We ought to have that down on the table. January the… 14th or 15th. Wait a minute, it's on my watch. If I can see my eyes up there. 15th. 1970. I always forget what year it is in January. I got to do it myself. The fun of how it happened, I was over there trying to park my car and Joe was outside, said to me, man, you're just the right guy. You came in town. You're just at St. Paul Reigns, see? Right. Maybe Joe's gone. Maybe Raymond knows.

Well, I'll tell you how to get the book, I can give you the address. Give me a call at work and I'll give you the address of the people that put the book out. You know what I'm saying? I don't know. I don't know. I don't know if they ever sent them back or anything. I don't know if they ever sent them back or anything. Maybe Joe's gone. Maybe Raymond knows. You know, I might have to write it up and mail it to you. You don't speak German, I imagine. No, Spanish.
Are you a family Spanish?

My brother went to Spain last year, see? He went to the fruit for me in New York. You can put the trailer there. Came there, based, and went to the fruit that was red, you know? All my people in Spain. Put it right there. You were born here though. Yeah. My brother was Spain last year. It was last year. Do you mind my asking your birthday?
We can get right on with this stuff. Oh no, of course not.
May the 20th. I'm getting young all the time.
Yeah.
And what part of town were you born in?

Well, now I'll tell you, that's a long story, since you asked me a question. Yeah, okay. Now, truth is speaking, I don't believe in lying about nothing I'd say. So, you asked me kind of a sort of a first question. I said, no, as a matter of fact, I wasn't born here. I wasn't born, I wasn't born here, you see? I was born in Mexico. In Mexico? Right. What part? Oh, about 100 miles from Mexico City, and Jalisco. Oh, that's where all the Mariachis came from. Where I saw her, where I saw her, where I saw her. See, my daddy and my mom were Spanish. I was born over there, and then he moved here, so. Was he a musician, your father? No, no. Mother? No. But I'll tell you what, I suggest to me this question. My mother's uncle directed the New York Symphony, his name was Chavez, C-H-V-E-Z, Carlos Chavez.
Oh, I'm not who he is.
I've heard his records. That's right. Well, my mom was first cut.
Well, he's a well-known musician, for sure.

I had his picture at all the office somewhere. I had one of my mother's brother's picture in history. We had this big orchestra in Mexico City, the biggest band I ever had there. I went out, of course, and not know jazz, of course. No. Long hair music, you know. Did you ever hear any of his music? Oh, yeah. Sure. Did you own any of his records? No, I don't hear any. Do you own a record for him?
Yeah, right there.
A couple of them. Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah. A lot of musicians don't own a record.

Well, I do. As a matter of fact, I had a lot of records. Raymond Boyd, you know, Raymond Will. I've known Raymond for years. He's come around my house. He says, you got some nice records in town? I said, yeah, I had a record box. Big Spider-Bank, Wolverine Band, Tylan Blues, Roy Gordon, all those records. He's come to my house, see. I said, big record box full of records, see, and arranged to come around and hear my records, see. I go to his house, see. And you know, I thought that doesn't get any recognition in the jazz club. And the class I was saying to me that I'm the only man she ever heard praising other drum, see. That's the way I am. God's good, he's good, see. To me, they got the top drum in New Orleans, boy. I live at it.
I've heard many, many musicians say that, and I don't think that the general public understood what he was doing. Very tough, man. Tops.

It's a funny thing, Dick. I got started playing drums. I'm doing vacation. I got a little job in the field, you see. Delivery boy, bundle boy. And Leo was my driver, but I didn't know he played drums, man. So, I used to call him Jazzy Leo all the time. I wonder why they call him that. When he come out to cash, turning the cash in. A little fat Irishman. He beat his hand on the table, fast. I said, man. So, one day, it was a pace drum in the truck, see. Truck like a pace, fancy. No, no pound truck that they have now, you know. I'm going way back, see. And I said, what's that a little drum? He said, I'll be stupid, bossy drums. I said, what are you doing with it, Leo? He said, I play it. What are you doing? Man, it's great. I wish I could play it. He gave a pair of sticks, see. So, I went out to his house. He had a set of drums sitting in his house. I said, I may he play some, Leo. He said, I know, man. He made a roll like tearing paper, man. I said, that's all. That's it, man. Good. So, I didn't have any drums, see. So, I made up a little, out of a cheese box. And I put a good skin on, see. I used to price, you know. Then I took less from my uncle, you know, with the old man Peterson, you know. Well, I wasn't playing drums. I don't think I was playing over, maybe six months. In those days, you can verify, I ask another musician. They can't music still right off what Gus Myers, you know. They still buy the hangout, they see. Everybody. Musicians. So, I sat there one day, and I, well, I used to, I always go around musicians all the time, see. So, and after that, everybody took it for granted. I was a musician. I was trying to be one. So, Peg said to me, you're working Saturday night? I was working any night. I said, no, man. I had no attitude, you know. Oh, yeah. So, I said, well, I got a little job. I said, well, I had Pinky at the Padre Roy, you know. So, I played that. I mean, I was just, this was back in 19, what was 1925? I was sick, boy. It was way back in that time, see. Then, in later years, I played with the Padre Roy with Pinky. The Doc of it, too.
Yeah.

Billy was with WWL singing, see, and he had another job at night in another place. He did, Billy. So, I was playing with Pinky, see. See, Pinky and I used to double date, see, with Bertha, you know. With Bertha, you know. With no challenge, you know. Bertha's too, see. So, that's how I got involved with the music. And, in those days, New Orleans, you know, they had a lot of house parties, you know. I'd brought pianos, you know. Uh-huh. Some homebrew, you know, bring the band in, that's it, see. So, that's how I got started to playin'. And, one time I was playing at the Slipper. I believe, uh, Dave Weinstein, I'm president right now. And, of course, Dave Weinstein, he was a good musician. He didn't read, you know. I couldn't read. I only could read on the song with the title of the song. Yeah. It was Echoes from Ireland, man. And, they had a piano player with a name, because you know him, you know everybody. Uh, Buzzi Weinstein, you know. Uh-huh. I was doing fine, man, until the song came in. I knew where it was, you know. I couldn't read, see. He says, man, I kept, I played on the song, you know. Uh-huh. So, everybody said, yeah, that's all of that, man. So, I looked there, I said, play it. And, I heard, with the right hand, you know, bass. With the right hand, hit the fifth, on the piano. You know, I don't know, it's coach, you see. I'm playin'. So, I played, see. So, right there, they gave me an idea. Go and take lessons. I go to Uncle, Mr. Peterson, see. So, I go out there, and he said to me, yeah. You know, he says, you were, I used to go to Raymond's boy, Ray Paducah, three of us, see. That's how I went on Raymond. Mm-hmm. Take lessons out there, see. Talk to jazz, but, ta-ta-ta-ta-ta. I couldn't get that, see. I get tired of business, and he hummed it with the violin, you know. When he hummed it to me, like, they go, ta-ta-ta-ta-ta. Yeah, man, you know. Ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta. Yeah, man. He said, don't try and fake. He said, read it. Count it with me. He said, oh, man. After that, I started playin' during the, uh, the WPA days. We had a big band, WS&B, you know. We had a staff band, you know. And as a matter of fact, I was wondering why they got me to go there. Because the guy in there was a fine drummer, man. He's the only living, guy that's living today, a musician. He got drummer. It's Pascal, you got. Fine drummer. He's about to live it, put it right to you. So, I got down. I said, Parson, what's the one with me here? The guy could read anything, you know. So, I said, now, the idea is this. When he got the band down, the ones that might, they could push the band, you know. So, I said, you know. A little more pushing, Parson, you know. So, I was in the band, so. I used to come home with this, uh, Harry Hopkins, you know, band and all that jazz. We'd play at 12 o'clock, WS&B.
Harry Hopkins, I don't remember him.
Well, he's at the WP, the WP National, all over the countries. I see. He and Roosevelt like that.
Oh, yeah, you mean Harry Hopkins from Washington.

Well, sure. The bass shot, man. It was us. Uh, Secretary of Interior. Uh-huh. Harry Lickish, you know. Oh, yeah. And the guy who had the, uh, the N.O. Ray, uh, Holly Johnson. Well, I mean, I'm kind of a historian myself, you know. Yeah, you know. Besides the music, you know. The foot. Pardon? You talk about, oh, yeah, this is what I want to mention, but it was to you. Uh-huh. I don't think hardly anybody has ever mentioned the foot and dance hall. Not yet, yeah. Which, every musician in town played at the foot and dance hall, you know. Everybody. Uh-huh. Well, I played there when it was called the Buckhorn on Burgundy Street. Uh-huh. One-twenty-five Burgundy.
Called the what?

The Buckhorn? The Buckhorn. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. The chief was a long chief of police and Captain Harry Drexel. I played in there. I took Van Gaiman's place. The only two drummers played in there was Van Gaiman and me. I took Van's place. As a matter of fact, how they came about. I said, I want to get to you straight. You can't do somebody else. It's difficult, but I'm telling you it's the real truth. Van was a fine drummer. I used to go play for Van Gaiman. One time there, Steve Lloyd Kean, a good promoter. He got the best job in town. He was a slipper. He was a slipper. He'd slip up to a fine band. He tried about two or three drummers and he couldn't cut the mustard. There was a reason. So I told Steve, I said, we were on the New St. Neville, right next door Steve's house on Kamp Street. I said, Steve, I'm going to go find a fine drummer. He said, yeah, but you got to read. I said, this guy could read anything. I used to go by the South Spine and I played together snare drum and did the music up there. I knew what he could do. He said, where's he playing? He laughed and I said, man, the four and the answer are all, man. I think at that time they had a, I forget, Shawy already left, see, with Tony Amarillo's playing trumpet. And he came over there and heard Van play. So then he brought him to Rehorsen. So I was very interested in how he made out, see, I noticed he make it, see. Steve, how he make out. He's fine, man. I hate it, see. So Van said to me, man, give me his job before, see. I had the job before, Van, with Steve, see. I told him, oh, Van, have you ever met Van Dam? Oh, yeah. He's a nice fellow. And Van said, hey, Van, I'm young and he, Van, see. I said, you want a good job? He's wondering why I didn't take it, see. Well, I got a job. Why don't you take it? He says, I'm not good enough. I said, I can't really good enough. Can you give me the job? He said, yeah. So I got the job from Steve, see. So I went to the front. So for about a week, all the drums come up and I want to play the drum. He said, ah, Monk was just beginning to learn how to play the peck on, you know, Monk, you know. I said, go on, man, play some drums for Monk. Oh, man, I want to play the drum, man, see. I want to play the peck on, see. And they said, learn it. And what else? He played the peck on, see. And so after that, everybody said, where's Van? Oh, he's taking a few nights off, you know. My job is over at my job, see. So Van said, I can't keep this up, you know. The guy's going to play for him, sit in for him, man, Leo. Leo's playing with Abbey Brunner at the halfway house, see. But he's going to play for me for kicks, you know. Leo, Ray, Purdue. I'll tell you another good drum. Remember Rod? You ever hear of him, Rod? I'm never. No, no, I didn't know him.
I knew Buck is the one.

Yeah, well Buck took my place. You see, this is recently. I compare it to the recent, at the famous door, see. There are two bands there. I remember Santa and the old man Christian. You know what I mean. It's a drum one place, see. I said, well, I didn't need anybody to call me up and all that. I said, so I went home from the barbershop and the phone and it was him. I'm going to come out to the famous door and play with the Dukes, you know. I said, what happened to Rod? I said, heart attack. Quiet, when I heard that. I said, man, I'm working to make it, man. I said, man, I'm looking for an old time drum. I said, get Buck Rogers. And they got Buck and Buck died too. I said, uh-oh. I swear.
Well, Emmett Rogers was different from Buck, huh?
Yeah, Emmett was out. Emmett played left hand drums, see. Yeah.
Snatsy Rogers.
Snatsy Rogers. Snatsy Rogers. Emmett played left hand like Monk, you know. That's why he comes to it.
I just watch him.
Except Monk played left, Monk played like this, you know. Monk played this drum on the left side, see. I put mine over here, see. Monk played over here. You play left footed or right footed? Me?
Right foot. Right foot and left handed. I play this, see.
Yeah, just like Monk, huh?
Yeah, huh.
And Emmett played with the drum upside down like this, see. Like that. And then like that, see. And I'll play the other way.
We better get everybody's name down.
I was thinking maybe you might want to look at some pictures, would you? Oh, yeah.
But let's get your name down so we can tell who you are. Can you give us your name? My name is Dick Allen, hers is Betty Rankin. Betty Rankin.
Claire Gutierrez.
And you got a middle name? I mean a maiden name?
Yes, Claire Perry Gutierrez. Claire Perry.
But you're kind of the Petersons too.
My mother was a Cassard. Her mother was a Cassard.
Yes.
And Jules Cassard was her brother and he wrote Angry. And he's getting royalties. Yeah, he's living in Florida and he's getting royalties on Angry.
Still following the horses?
I believe he does that in the winter. Oh. He's retired now.
Oh, yeah.

And I'm also related to Raymond Burke and Harold Peterson and George Peterson. My grandfather was Jules Cassard, played the violin in the French Opera. And he taught Uncle George Peterson. Taught him the violin and drum. And then he married his daughter.
And then George Peterson's son is Harold?
Right. His son is Harold and then there's little Harold who has the music of Moods band.
It's hard for me to keep all that family straight. Well... Oh, can be gentle.

There were about eight or nine children, you see. And Raymond Burke's mother was one of the Cassard girls. Harold Peterson's mother was one of the Cassards and my mother was a Cassard. There were only those girls. And there was a Joe Cassard. That's right. And that's her brother, Joe Cassard. Captain Cassard. And he was captain of the police. The police. And Jules and, let's see, Lucian and Leo, Leo Cassard.
He didn't know Cass, Joe the Cass, the banjo player. The mother boy, yeah.
I never met him.
I've heard of him. Joe had Raymond mentioned him.

I think I've seen his picture with him. Sure, he was Raymond. He told me, but he had a stroke and he's in a coma. He's been in a coma for about two or three years. But he was a terrific banjo player, guitar player.
Let's see, Leo played banjo. Jules played bass and trombone and maybe piano.

Jules played most everything. Anything. He played piano too. He told us he rolled on the floor with the bass one night because he didn't know how to play it and he just hammed it up. And then Joe played guitar and sang. Bertie played piano. And Roni played piano. That's Raymond's mother. My mother didn't play in musical instruments. And the grandfather was the one who played in the French opera. He played French horn and violin and hornet, I believe. They used to have a party just when they'd get together.
Oh, yeah. But Raymond was a barrier also, isn't it?
Well, Raymond's mother was married before and then she married Mr. Burke and he adopted Raymond.
I see. And so, then, I don't know, were any of Raymond's brothers musical or anything? No.
Nobody in the family. Raymond was more musical than the rest of them. They sing but they're not aggressive.
I'll tell you about Raymond.

Harold Peterson's sister, Lucille Peterson, was killed up in New Jersey. She played with a girl's band. She had gold saxophone. And then his other sister, May Seal, she played with an orchestra and my sister played called Shades of Blue when they were young.
They have another one.
Lucille.
Imagine off and cycle with a band on there. All five drumming.

But May Seal and my sister had played with a little Galadora girl and they had a little orchestra about 20, 30 years ago when they were young. Nine people. But it was here. Yes. It didn't do so well because all the boys would stand in front of the girls where they'd play music and wouldn't dance with the rest of the girls. Well, I was in a band.
I was in a band. I was in a band. But it was pretty though.

It was pretty though. They had blue velvet dresses and they had, that was their theme song, Late in the Evening. That's right. And then there was a nine piece orchestra. It was a beautiful band, but they didn't do too much for that reason. How many girls in the band? Nine. It was like that. You would play with them?
I played with them. Like Betty Hutton.
I played with them in that band. My sister played drum and then Sal played drum. My sister, Lice Perry, Lice Bajon.
I was the only guy in the band with eight women in the family. A lot of music in the family.
Oh, and Rose Cassard sang too. That's old Joe Cassard, his daughter sang. There's a lot of music in the family.
She can sing too, man.
Oh. Every Christmas at the office I get up and sing on the stage.
One night we had a band boy and she was singing up there. Brought the house down and we played somewhere. Why haven't we played? Joe Brown's place in Bulldogs in there.
Broadwater. What's the way of Beach? Edge. Edge. Edgewater called. Is it Broadwater Beach?
Yeah, the one that Joe Brown knows.
Edgewater is where the rich people go and Broadwater is more fun place.

Oh, but the one you're talking about, the big hotel years ago, when I was playing in Biloxi, I was playing with, I believe, with Alex Spatic of the Trauma. I played in some way. And Johnny Quattusi, he was a collected dues for the union for 174 in Biloxi. At that time they had the name bands in this hotel here. And Johnny Bajon was playing the band. See Johnny? Nobody gives a guy any credit. He was playing with the best man, Johnny Bajon. I don't know that. He was playing with the band, Joe Lief was playing. Big band, about four volumes in the band, old man. That's the guy Mr. Johnny was, see. Poor Johnny was nothing or nothing. I don't know what happened to him. But I'm telling you, one time, he was the top man. I live in here Sharky. I ring with the brother, I'm in here Sharky. He said, man, you're a band by Johnny. I want you to hear Sharky play. I'm about to do a man in Taunty. He's up there when he was young, he was the head up there, left hand in the handkerchief, playing Panama. You know, all that stuff. I've been here Johnny, the awful man's rag man, up at the Arcadia on the Canale, the burgundy upstairs in 1923, I believe, 22. Johnny, he could play some corn and then he played in Chicago to Chicago theater. He used to do it for the musicians. He built the best, Frank and Masters, you know. See Johnny? He didn't talk. But I know where he played. What about Joe Boycannon? What?
What about Joe Boycannon? Oh, well I see.
A lot of fellas that don't get mentioned at all, wouldn't really play, see. I noticed that. You're talking about which one?
Steve's brother, the one that just died.
The saxophone.
Right. The bass, beautiful.
We used to go up there on Monday nights and play and sing, you know.

You know one time, excuse me, in a jazz club, a jazz club, when the book was put out, there's a picture in there and it gives the names of the fellas in the band. And it says, on drums, Monk Hazel. Monk was nowhere near the place. Monk didn't play drums in his band. Lee Wilder played drums because I got ahead of the jazz myself. Went to the sky to the mountain in New York. Fred Norman on the piano. Bill Hillen playing trumpet. He kind of played like Bixson those days, Bill Hillen. I never met him.
I know you've heard of him.
But you heard of him?
Yeah.
Allman used to play with him. That's right. Well, I was playing in the band, see. At the point, allman played piano and Billy played trumpet.
Used to play it.
Just like Bix, man. And here they went to New York and lay on drums. Not Monk Hazel. I said, drum, Monk. He was nowhere near that.
Tell him how long you know Arm and Hope.
I got a picture of him. I used to play ball. I was kids, man. Allman.
Well, where were you born? I mean, where did you live in town here when you first came?
About a large kind of right there, 1545 Camp Street.

And how old were you when you came to town? I was about seven years old. About seven years old. So you knew all that gang around that neighborhood? Everybody. Around that Coliseum Square and all? Yeah.

Raps came to them and played guitar out there, man. I said to them to play guitar, rap, and Paul too. Joe's brother. I didn't know Joe then, you know. Paul Morris. Yeah, I knew Paul. Then in Chicago, when I played Fry's Inn, I used to go up there. Used to go up to Fry's Inn?
That's right, in Chicago.
I walked back to Van Buren.
But what did you do to get up there? Were you on vacation working?

I went up there in the half building, Chicago. I was at the Palmer House, I was at the Morrison, the Drake. And I played a few honky-tonks myself. So I mean, like I tell you, I see a lot of stuff that people talk about, and I know they don't want to talk about it because they've never been there, see?
Well, tell me about Paul. Did he play much here in town, Paul Morat?
Paul Morat? No, he...
That's something I don't know what they're in here about.

No, I'll tell you about Paul. Paul don't play too much in town. He played on, which was the later year, it was called the Foreign Dance Store, 10-15 I would go, see? They played Paul and Rap and Oscar Marco, see? Then they went to Chicago and played at the Fry's Inn, the rhythm came up, that's when they made those records. They played the Tin Roof, Maple Leaf Rag, and Mellow Boy George, you know? That's when they got famous after, see? And the big shot like Benny Goodman, used to come around Fry's Inn to hear rap play, man. And I and Harry James to hear Paul play. Because Paul didn't have a lot of technique, see? All right. Paul would play when he drives, man. Used to modulate, go up to C-sharp on that last chorus of Mellow Boy George, man, he's about to drive, man. One like that, well Steve can tell you, Steve played banjo. On Rampart, I didn't turn the thing down. Rampart, but to tell me if I could Rampart, you know, show that, see? They had a father named a fighter, a violin, very exotic Greeks, right in front of the drum I was playing, you know? And this was a benefit dance to try to save a bit of rope, you know? So Steve played there, the rhythm came in, man. Steve was playing banjo. Steve and Leo Addy, Paul, I'll tell you another great musician. He does not mention too much, Alasdor Bourjom.
Oh, yeah.
He played the rhythm of the clarinet, man.
And John Vardar. I like his tenor and his bass sax, too, Alasdor.

You would? Yeah. Very fun. I really love his tenor playing. Fine, boy. Who started that style of tenor? I'm always curious about that, you know? There's so many guys that play that way. The style? Yeah, that many plays. So that style of saxophone doesn't have to be tenor.

I know what you mean. Well, I'll tell you, the first one I heard play like that was, a lot of people think, was Bostick, you know Bostick. Mm-hmm. Which, Samuel Terracopp's from Bostick. Mm-hmm. But the first guy I thought playing like that was a fella, maybe Armour could tell you that, too. I was playing with Don Redman, Colvin Hawkins. You know where the Hawkins is? Oh, yeah, I heard that. Montana. Hawkins playing tenor, Johnny Hodges playing Alton.
But it seems to me that before that, if I listen to the records, Eddie Powers was playing good, and Bordello.
Yeah, well, you know, there's another guy that doesn't mention much, Charlie Codello. Yeah. I see Charlie all the time.
I never met Lester Nelson, and I never heard him. What was he like? I was playing with Lester and Harry, man. I'm sure that's a bitch.
Yeah.

Get it. I was playing this place here with Lester Nelson and Harry Schuyl was playing. I was playing the drum. Yeah. I see.

What kind of music does he write? I don't know whether...is it rock and roll sound? Well, yeah, it's a rock and roll. I don't know. But at the worst night, the music player...

I don't know. I don't know. I don't know.
I don't know.
Maybe he wants to.
Where was his name?

Yeah, we were playing a little get-together up there, you know. A fun, free job, you know, and I just playing tenor. And then I got up there, I was playing a little play. I was playing a little play. I was playing a little play. I was playing a little play. I was playing a little play. I was telling Eddie sometimes to come back in a speech. I'm talking to Eddie and snap the pictures.

Eddie at the front, yeah. At the front, yeah. At the front, mm-hmm. Yeah, I was passionate to get married, Eddie, man.
Eddie Miller. That's right.

He's playing a lot. At the gym hotel, he's playing a sound when he saw him. Eddie Miller. I got Eddie Miller and Fazz Ola, the first job I ever had at the front dance on both of them. And Eddie played better. In those days, Eddie played better clarinet than Fazz. And Fazz played better, I mean, and Eddie played better tenor than Fazz. So he swapped around, see. And we had Eddie Miller and Fazz at the same time in the front, see. And we had a good kick in the back, man. Wasn't Bill Bourgeois in there at one time, too? Well, Bourgeois played that before then.
